:::

---

## 5.1 Point Estimates and Interval Estimates

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Point estimate**

A single numerical value computed from sample data that serves as the best guess of an unknown population parameter.

Examples: $\bar{x}$ estimates $\mu$, $s^2$ estimates $\sigma^2$, and $\hat p$ estimates $p$.
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Confidence interval**

A plausible range of values for a population parameter, built from sample data and a specified confidence level.
:::
::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Big idea.** A statistic will usually not equal the parameter exactly. The interval tells us how far away the statistic could reasonably be.
:::

---

## The CI Skeleton

::: {.defbox}
All confidence intervals in this chapter are variations of:

$$
\text{estimate} \pm
\underbrace{(\text{critical value})(\text{standard error})}_{\text{margin of error}}
$$
:::

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Estimate</span>
$\bar{x}$, $\hat p$, $\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2$, $\hat p_1-\hat p_2$, $s^2$, or $s_1^2/s_2^2$.
:::
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Critical value</span>
From $Z$, $t$, $\chi^2$, or $F$, depending on the sampling distribution.
:::
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Standard error</span>
The standard deviation of the estimator, or an estimate of it.
:::
::::

---

## 5.2 Interpreting Confidence

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
For a $C\%$ confidence interval:

In repeated sampling, about $C\%$ of intervals constructed using this method will capture the true parameter.
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
Do not say: "There is a 95% probability that this particular interval contains $\mu$."

The parameter is fixed. The random object is the interval produced by the sample.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.ci-sim-plot}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4.5
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| out-width: "430px"
set.seed(10)
n <- 50
num_sims <- 50
true_mu <- 0
z <- qnorm(0.975)
ci_df <- data.frame(sim = 1:num_sims) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(
    sample = list(rnorm(n, true_mu, 1)),
    mean = mean(unlist(sample)),
    se = sd(unlist(sample)) / sqrt(n),
    lower = mean - z * se,
    upper = mean + z * se,
    misses = lower > true_mu | upper < true_mu
  ) |>
  ungroup()

ci_df <- ci_df |>
  mutate(
    colour = if_else(misses, "#f9a825", "#00695c"),
    status = if_else(misses, "Misses true mean", "Covers true mean"),
    hover = paste0(
      "<b>Simulation ", sim, "</b>",
      "<br>Interval: [", round(lower, 3), ", ", round(upper, 3), "]",
      "<br>Status: ", status
    )
  )

plot_ly(width = 430, height = 320) |>
  add_segments(
    data = ci_df,
    x = ~lower,
    xend = ~upper,
    y = ~sim,
    yend = ~sim,
    color = ~status,
    colors = c("Covers true mean" = "#00695c", "Misses true mean" = "#f9a825"),
    line = list(width = 4),
    text = ~hover,
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>",
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  layout(
    autosize = FALSE,
    width = 430,
    height = 320,
    margin = list(l = 48, r = 8, t = 10, b = 42),
    xaxis = list(
      title = "Interval endpoints",
      zeroline = FALSE,
      showgrid = TRUE,
      gridcolor = "#e8e8e8"
    ),
    yaxis = list(
      title = "Simulation",
      showticklabels = FALSE,
      zeroline = FALSE,
      showgrid = TRUE,
      gridcolor = "#e8e8e8"
    ),
    shapes = list(
      list(
        type = "line",
        x0 = true_mu,
        x1 = true_mu,
        y0 = 0.5,
        y1 = num_sims + 0.5,
        line = list(color = "#004d40", width = 2, dash = "dash")
      )
    ),
    showlegend = FALSE,
    paper_bgcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0)",
    plot_bgcolor = "white"
  ) |>
  config(displayModeBar = FALSE, responsive = FALSE)
```
:::
:::
::::

---

## CI Reference Guide

| Target parameter | Situation | Reference distribution | Interval shape |
|---|---|---:|---|
| $\mu$ | one mean, $\sigma$ known | $Z$ | $\bar{x}\pm z^*\sigma/\sqrt n$ |
| $\mu$ | one mean, $\sigma$ unknown | $t_{n-1}$ | $\bar{x}\pm t^*s/\sqrt n$ |
| $p$ | one proportion | $Z$ | $\hat p\pm z^*\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$ |
| $\sigma^2$ | one variance, normal population | $\chi^2_{n-1}$ | asymmetric |
| $\mu_1-\mu_2$ | two independent means | $Z$ or $t$ | difference $\pm$ margin |
| $p_1-p_2$ | two independent proportions | $Z$ | difference $\pm$ margin |
| $\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2$ | ratio of variances | $F$ | asymmetric |
| $\mu_d$ | paired data | $t_{n-1}$ | $\bar d\pm t^*s_d/\sqrt n$ |

---

## Quick Critical Values

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.col}
| Confidence level | $z^*$ |
|:--:|:--:|
| 90% | 1.645 |
| 95% | 1.960 |
| 99% | 2.576 |

::: {.notebox}
<span class="label">R check</span>
`qnorm(0.95)`, `qnorm(0.975)`, and `qnorm(0.995)` give these values.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

qnorm(c(0.95, 0.975, 0.995))

# For t, chi-square, and F values:
qt(0.975, df = 9)
qchisq(c(0.025, 0.975), df = 24)
qf(c(0.025, 0.975), df1 = 9, df2 = 11)
```
:::
::::

## 5.3.1 Interactive One-Mean Calculator

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
::: {.ci-widget}
<label for="ci-mode">Interval type</label>
<select id="ci-mode" onchange="updateCiCalc()">
  <option value="z">Known sigma: z interval</option>
  <option value="t">Unknown sigma: t interval</option>
</select>
<label for="ci-xbar">Sample mean</label>
<input id="ci-xbar" type="number" value="68.6" step="0.1" oninput="updateCiCalc()">
<label for="ci-spread">Sigma or sample sd</label>
<input id="ci-spread" type="number" value="15" step="0.1" oninput="updateCiCalc()">
<label for="ci-n">Sample size</label>
<input id="ci-n" type="number" value="15" step="1" min="2" oninput="updateCiCalc()">
<label for="ci-conf">Confidence level</label>
<select id="ci-conf" onchange="updateCiCalc()">
  <option value="0.90">90%</option>
  <option value="0.95" selected>95%</option>
  <option value="0.99">99%</option>
</select>
<div id="ci-output" class="ci-result"></div>
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.thinkbox}
Try changing the confidence level. The estimate stays fixed, but the critical value and margin of error change.
:::

::: {.notebox}
<span class="label">Calculator note</span>
The $t$ option uses a small built-in table for common confidence levels and degrees of freedom. Use R for exact values.
:::
:::
::::

<script>
function ciZ(conf) {
  if (conf === 0.90) return 1.645;
  if (conf === 0.95) return 1.96;
  return 2.576;
}
function ciT(conf, df) {
  var table = {
    "0.90":[6.314,2.920,2.353,2.132,2.015,1.943,1.895,1.860,1.833,1.812,1.796,1.782,1.771,1.761,1.753,1.746,1.740,1.734,1.729,1.725,1.721,1.717,1.714,1.711,1.708,1.706,1.703,1.701,1.699,1.697],
    "0.95":[12.706,4.303,3.182,2.776,2.571,2.447,2.365,2.306,2.262,2.228,2.201,2.179,2.160,2.145,2.131,2.120,2.110,2.101,2.093,2.086,2.080,2.074,2.069,2.064,2.060,2.056,2.052,2.048,2.045,2.042],
    "0.99":[63.657,9.925,5.841,4.604,4.032,3.707,3.499,3.355,3.250,3.169,3.106,3.055,3.012,2.977,2.947,2.921,2.898,2.878,2.861,2.845,2.831,2.819,2.807,2.797,2.787,2.779,2.771,2.763,2.756,2.750]
  };
  if (df <= 30) return table[conf.toFixed(2)][df - 1];
  return ciZ(conf);
}
window.updateCiCalc = function () {
  var mode = document.getElementById("ci-mode").value;
  var xbar = Number(document.getElementById("ci-xbar").value);
  var spread = Number(document.getElementById("ci-spread").value);
  var n = Number(document.getElementById("ci-n").value);
  var conf = Number(document.getElementById("ci-conf").value);
  var critical = mode === "z" ? ciZ(conf) : ciT(conf, Math.max(1, Math.round(n - 1)));
  var se = spread / Math.sqrt(n);
  var moe = critical * se;
  document.getElementById("ci-output").innerHTML =
    "Critical value: " + critical.toFixed(3) + "<br>" +
    "SE: " + se.toFixed(4) + "<br>" +
    "CI: (" + (xbar - moe).toFixed(4) + ", " + (xbar + moe).toFixed(4) + ")";
};
setTimeout(updateCiCalc, 500);
</script>

## 5.3.1.1 One Mean, Known $\sigma$

::: {.defbox}
When the population standard deviation $\sigma$ is known:

$$
\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}
$$

Use this for a population mean $\mu$ with known $\sigma$.
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Assumptions</span>

<ul class="assumption-list">
  <li class="fragment">Random sample or randomized experiment.</li>
  <li class="fragment">Independent observations.</li>
  <li class="fragment">Population is normal, or $n$ is large enough for the CLT.</li>
</ul>
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Exam cue</span>
If the problem gives a population standard deviation, use $z$. If it gives a sample standard deviation, use $t$.
:::
::::

---

## Example: Known Sigma - Magazine Readers {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
Playbill magazine reports $\bar{x}=119{,}155$ dollars from $n=80$ households. Assume $\sigma=30{,}000$ dollars.

Construct 90%, 95%, and 99% confidence intervals for the population mean household income of readers.
:::

| Level | Critical value | Margin of error | Confidence interval |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| 90% | 1.645 | $1.645(30000/\sqrt{80})=5517.38$ | $(113637.62, 124672.38)$ |
| 95% | 1.960 | $1.960(30000/\sqrt{80})=6573.04$ | $(112581.96, 125728.04)$ |
| 99% | 2.576 | $2.576(30000/\sqrt{80})=8640.41$ | $(110514.59, 127795.41)$ |

::: {.examplebox}
We are 95% confident that the mean household income of Playbill readers is between about 112,582 dollars and 125,728 dollars.
:::

---

## Example: Known Sigma - Car Sales {.scrollable}

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.taskbox}
Annual car sales are normally distributed with known $\sigma=15$. For a random sample of 15 salespeople:

$$79,43,58,66,101,63,79,33,58,71,60,101,74,55,88$$

Construct a 95% CI for $\mu$.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

cars <- c(79,43,58,66,101,63,79,33,58,71,60,101,74,55,88)
xbar <- mean(cars)
n <- length(cars)
sigma <- 15
zstar <- qnorm(0.975)
ci <- xbar + c(-1, 1) * zstar * sigma / sqrt(n)

xbar
ci
```
:::
::::

::: {.examplebox}
$\bar{x}=68.6$, so the interval is approximately $(61.01, 76.19)$. We are 95% confident that the population mean number of cars sold annually is between about 61 and 76.
:::

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

A sample has $\bar{x}=42$, $n=36$, and known $\sigma=12$. For a 95% CI, what is the margin of error?
::::

- 1.96
- [3.92]{.correct data-explanation="The standard error is 12/sqrt(36)=2. For 95% confidence, z*=1.96, so the margin of error is 1.96 times 2 = 3.92."}
- 4.00
- 7.84

---

## 5.3.1.2 One Mean, Unknown $\sigma$

::: {.defbox}
When $\sigma$ is unknown, estimate it with $s$ and use the Student $t$ distribution:

$$
\bar{x} \pm t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\frac{s}{\sqrt n}
$$
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.notebox}
<span class="label">Why t?</span>
Replacing $\sigma$ with $s$ adds uncertainty. The $t$ distribution has heavier tails, especially for small degrees of freedom.
:::

::: {.warnbox}
<span class="label">Small samples</span>
For small $n$, check that the population is reasonably normal or that the sample has no severe skew/outliers.
:::
::::

---

## Example: Unknown Sigma - Ancient Air {.scrollable}

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.taskbox}
Nitrogen percentages from air bubbles trapped in ancient amber:

$$63.4,65.0,64.4,63.3,54.8,64.5,60.8,49.1,51.0$$

Construct a 90% CI for the mean nitrogen percentage.
:::

::: {.examplebox}
Using $n=9$, $\bar{x}=59.5889$, $s=6.2553$, and $t^*=1.8595$:

$$59.5889\pm1.8595\frac{6.2553}{3}=(55.71,63.47).$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

nitrogen <- c(63.4,65.0,64.4,63.3,54.8,64.5,60.8,49.1,51.0)
t.test(nitrogen, conf.level = 0.90)
```
:::
::::

---

## Example: Unknown Sigma - Camera Photos {.scrollable}

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.taskbox}
A random sample of 10 digital camera owners has stored photo counts:

$$25,6,22,26,31,18,13,20,14,2$$

Construct a 95% CI for the population mean number of stored photos.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

photos <- c(25,6,22,26,31,18,13,20,14,2)
mean(photos)
sd(photos)
t.test(photos, conf.level = 0.95)
```
:::
::::

::: {.examplebox}
$\bar{x}=17.7$, $s=9.0805$, $df=9$, and $t^*=2.262$. The 95% CI is approximately $(11.20,24.20)$ photos.
:::

---

## 5.3.2 One Proportion

::: {.defbox}
For a population proportion $p$, with $\hat p=x/n$:

$$
\hat p \pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}
$$
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Conditions</span>

<ul class="assumption-list">
  <li class="fragment">Random sample.</li>
  <li class="fragment">Independent Bernoulli trials.</li>
  <li class="fragment">Large counts: $n\hat p \ge 10$ and $n(1-\hat p)\ge 10$.</li>
</ul>
:::
::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Boundary check</span>
The final interval should make sense for a proportion. Values below 0 or above 1 need careful handling.
:::
::::

---

## Example: One Proportion - Transit Use {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
A university survey asks 1200 students whether they use public transportation. Among them, 738 say yes.

Construct a 95% CI for the true proportion of students who use public transportation.
:::

$$
\hat p=\frac{738}{1200}=0.6150
$$

$$
SE=\sqrt{\frac{0.6150(0.3850)}{1200}}=0.01405
$$

$$
0.6150\pm1.96(0.01405)=(0.5875,0.6425)
$$

::: {.examplebox}
We are 95% confident that between 58.75% and 64.25% of students use public transportation.
:::

---

## Example: One Proportion - Work From Home {.scrollable}

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.taskbox}
In a survey of 650 employees, 286 prefer working from home at least three days per week.

Construct a 90% CI for the population proportion.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

x <- 286
n <- 650
phat <- x / n
zstar <- qnorm(0.95)
se <- sqrt(phat * (1 - phat) / n)
phat + c(-1, 1) * zstar * se
```
:::
::::

::: {.examplebox}
$\hat p=0.44$, so the 90% CI is approximately $(0.4079,0.4721)$.
:::

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

For a one-proportion confidence interval, which sample has enough successes and failures for the normal approximation?
::::

- $n=20$, $\hat p=0.90$
- $n=50$, $\hat p=0.10$
- [$n=100$, $\hat p=0.20$]{.correct data-explanation="This gives n phat = 20 and n(1-phat)=80, both at least 10."}
- $n=15$, $\hat p=0.50$

## 5.3.3 One Variance

::: {.defbox}
For a normally distributed population, a confidence interval for $\sigma^2$ is:

$$
\left(
\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{\alpha/2,n-1}},
\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,n-1}}
\right)
$$
:::

::: {.warnbox}
This interval is asymmetric. Normality matters here much more than it does for large-sample mean intervals.
:::

---

## Example: One Variance - Bottle Filling {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
A random sample of 25 bottles has sample variance $s^2=12.5$. Assume filling amounts are normally distributed.

Construct a 95% CI for $\sigma^2$.
:::

$$df=24,\quad \chi^2_{0.975,24}=39.364,\quad \chi^2_{0.025,24}=12.401$$

$$
\text{Lower}=\frac{24(12.5)}{39.364}=7.62,\qquad
\text{Upper}=\frac{24(12.5)}{12.401}=24.19
$$

::: {.examplebox}
The 95% CI for the population variance is approximately $(7.62,24.19)$.
:::

---

## Example: One Variance - Reaction Times {.scrollable}

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.taskbox}
A random sample of 16 drivers has sample variance $s^2=0.36$. Assume reaction times are normally distributed.

Construct a 90% CI for $\sigma^2$.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

n <- 16
s2 <- 0.36
alpha <- 0.10
df <- n - 1
lower <- df * s2 / qchisq(1 - alpha / 2, df)
upper <- df * s2 / qchisq(alpha / 2, df)
c(lower, upper)
```
:::
::::

::: {.examplebox}
The 90% CI is approximately $(0.2160,0.7437)$.
:::

---

## 5.4.1.1 Two Means: Known $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$

::: {.defbox}
When both population standard deviations are known:

$$
(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)\pm z_{\alpha/2}
\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}
$$
:::

::: {.notebox}
<span class="label">Reality check</span>
This case is uncommon in practice because population standard deviations are rarely known. We will use two short worked examples, then focus on the more realistic $t$ intervals.
:::

---

## Example: Known Sigmas - Course Marks {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
Suppose final marks in the same course are compared between two campuses.

UTSG: $n_1=64$, $\bar{x}_1=76$, known $\sigma_1=10$.  
UTM: $n_2=81$, $\bar{x}_2=72$, known $\sigma_2=12$.

Construct a 95% CI for $\mu_1-\mu_2$.
:::

$$
\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2=4
$$

$$
SE=\sqrt{\frac{10^2}{64}+\frac{12^2}{81}}=1.827
$$

$$
4\pm1.96(1.827)=(0.42,7.58)
$$

::: {.examplebox}
We are 95% confident that the UTSG population mean is between 0.42 and 7.58 marks higher than the UTM population mean.
:::

---

## Example: Known Sigmas - Study Time {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
Two independent samples compare average weekly study time.

Group 1: $n_1=40$, $\bar{x}_1=12.4$, known $\sigma_1=3.2$.  
Group 2: $n_2=35$, $\bar{x}_2=10.9$, known $\sigma_2=2.8$.

Construct a 95% CI for $\mu_1-\mu_2$.
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

n1 <- 40; x1 <- 12.4; sigma1 <- 3.2
n2 <- 35; x2 <- 10.9; sigma2 <- 2.8

estimate <- x1 - x2
se <- sqrt(sigma1^2/n1 + sigma2^2/n2)
estimate + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se
```

::: {.examplebox}
The 95% CI is approximately $(0.14,2.86)$ hours. Group 1 appears to study more hours per week on average.
:::

---

## 5.4.1.3 Two Means: Equal Variances

::: {.defbox}
If the two population variances are unknown but assumed equal:

$$
(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)\pm t_{n_1+n_2-2,\alpha/2}
s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}}
$$

where

$$
s_p^2=\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2}.
$$
:::

---

## Example: Pooled t - Battery Brands {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
A researcher compares battery life for two brands of the same device.

Brand A: $n_1=12$, $\bar{x}_1=52.4$, $s_1=6.1$.  
Brand B: $n_2=10$, $\bar{x}_2=47.8$, $s_2=5.4$.

Assume equal population variances. Construct a 95% CI for $\mu_1-\mu_2$.
:::

$$
s_p^2=\frac{11(6.1^2)+9(5.4^2)}{20}=33.493,\quad s_p=5.787
$$

$$
SE=5.787\sqrt{\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{10}}=2.476,\quad t^*_{20}=2.086
$$

$$
4.6\pm2.086(2.476)=(-0.57,9.77)
$$

::: {.examplebox}
Because the interval contains 0, the data do not clearly show a nonzero mean battery-life difference.
:::

---

## Example: Pooled t - Tutorial Methods {.scrollable}

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.taskbox}
Method A: $n_1=15$, $\bar{x}_1=84.2$, $s_1=7.5$.  
Method B: $n_2=14$, $\bar{x}_2=78.6$, $s_2=6.8$.

Assume equal variances. Construct a 90% CI for $\mu_1-\mu_2$.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

n1 <- 15; x1 <- 84.2; s1 <- 7.5
n2 <- 14; x2 <- 78.6; s2 <- 6.8
sp2 <- ((n1-1)*s1^2 + (n2-1)*s2^2) / (n1+n2-2)
sp <- sqrt(sp2)
se <- sp * sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2)
tstar <- qt(0.95, df = n1+n2-2)
(x1-x2) + c(-1, 1) * tstar * se
```
:::
::::

::: {.examplebox}
The 90% CI is approximately $(1.06,10.14)$ points. Method A appears to have a higher mean quiz score.
:::

---

## 5.4.1.4 Two Means: Unequal Variances

::: {.defbox .fragment}
For unequal unknown variances, use Welch's interval:

$$
(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)\pm t_{df,\alpha/2}
\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}.
$$
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Degrees of freedom</span>
Software uses the Welch-Satterthwaite approximation. A conservative hand approximation is $df=\min(n_1-1,n_2-1)$.
:::

---

## Welch Degrees of Freedom

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">For hand work</span>
When the Welch formula is not the main point of the question, use the conservative degrees of freedom:

$$
df=\min(n_1-1,n_2-1).
$$
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
Software usually uses the Welch-Satterthwaite approximation:

$$
df=
\frac{
\left(\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{s_2^2}{n_2}\right)^2
}{
\frac{(s_1^2/n_1)^2}{n_1-1}
+
\frac{(s_2^2/n_2)^2}{n_2-1}
}.
$$
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
Welch is the better default when the population variances are unknown and equal variances are not clearly justified.
:::

---

## Example: Welch t - Commute Times {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
Group 1: $n_1=25$, $\bar{x}_1=42$, $s_1=14$.  
Group 2: $n_2=30$, $\bar{x}_2=35$, $s_2=9$.

Assume unequal variances. Construct a 95% CI for $\mu_1-\mu_2$.
:::

$$
SE=\sqrt{\frac{14^2}{25}+\frac{9^2}{30}}=3.245
$$

Using Welch $df\approx38.6$, $t^*\approx2.023$:

$$
7\pm2.023(3.245)=(0.43,13.57)
$$

::: {.examplebox}
The interval is entirely positive, suggesting Group 1 has a higher mean commute time.
:::

---

## Example: Welch t - Food Spending {.scrollable}

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.taskbox}
Group 1: $n_1=18$, $\bar{x}_1=96$, $s_1=22$.  
Group 2: $n_2=22$, $\bar{x}_2=82$, $s_2=16$.

Assume unequal variances. Construct a 90% CI for $\mu_1-\mu_2$.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

n1 <- 18; x1 <- 96; s1 <- 22
n2 <- 22; x2 <- 82; s2 <- 16
se <- sqrt(s1^2/n1 + s2^2/n2)
df <- (s1^2/n1 + s2^2/n2)^2 /
  ((s1^2/n1)^2/(n1-1) + (s2^2/n2)^2/(n2-1))
tstar <- qt(0.95, df)
(x1 - x2) + c(-1, 1) * tstar * se
df
```
:::
::::

::: {.examplebox}
The 90% CI is approximately $(3.47,24.53)$. Group 1 appears to have a higher mean weekly food spending.
:::

---

## 5.4.1.5 Two Means: Assumptions

:::: {.assumption-stack}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">For all two-sample mean CIs</span>

<ul class="assumption-list">
  <li class="fragment">The two samples are independent.</li>
  <li class="fragment">Each sample is random, or the data come from a randomized design.</li>
  <li class="fragment">Each population is approximately normal, or both samples are large enough for the CLT.</li>
</ul>
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Extra assumption for pooled t</span>

<ul class="assumption-list">
  <li class="fragment">Use the pooled interval only when equal population variances are reasonable.</li>
  <li class="fragment">If the equal-variance assumption is doubtful, use Welch's interval.</li>
</ul>
:::
::::

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

Two independent samples have unknown and clearly unequal sample standard deviations. Which interval is usually the best default for $\mu_1-\mu_2$?
::::

- Known-sigma $z$ interval
- Pooled two-sample $t$ interval
- [Welch two-sample $t$ interval]{.correct data-explanation="Welch's interval does not require the equal-variance assumption and is the usual default when population variances are unknown."}
- One-proportion $z$ interval

---

## 5.4.2 Difference of Proportions

::: {.defbox .fragment}
For two independent population proportions:

$$
(\hat p_1-\hat p_2)\pm z_{\alpha/2}
\sqrt{
\frac{\hat p_1(1-\hat p_1)}{n_1}
+
\frac{\hat p_2(1-\hat p_2)}{n_2}
}
$$
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
Check large counts in both groups: successes and failures should each be at least 10.
:::

---

## Example: Difference of Proportions - Left-Handed Students {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
Campus 1 has 18 left-handed students out of 120. Campus 2 has 10 left-handed students out of 100.

Construct a 95% CI for $p_1-p_2$.
:::

$$
\hat p_1=0.1500,\quad \hat p_2=0.1000,\quad \hat p_1-\hat p_2=0.0500
$$

$$
SE=\sqrt{\frac{0.15(0.85)}{120}+\frac{0.10(0.90)}{100}}=0.0443
$$

$$
0.05\pm1.96(0.0443)=(-0.0368,0.1368)
$$

::: {.examplebox}
The interval includes 0, so a zero difference in population proportions is plausible.
:::

---

## Example: Difference of Proportions - Policy Support {.scrollable}

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.taskbox}
City 1 has 210 supporters out of 500. City 2 has 170 supporters out of 450.

Construct a 90% CI for $p_1-p_2$.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

x1 <- 210; n1 <- 500
x2 <- 170; n2 <- 450
p1 <- x1/n1; p2 <- x2/n2
se <- sqrt(p1*(1-p1)/n1 + p2*(1-p2)/n2)
(p1 - p2) + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.95) * se
```
:::
::::

::: {.examplebox}
The 90% CI is approximately $(-0.010,0.095)$. Because 0 is inside, the data do not clearly establish a higher support rate for City 1.
:::

---

## 5.4.2.1 Difference of Proportions: Assumptions

:::: {.assumption-stack}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Sampling structure</span>

<ul class="assumption-list">
  <li class="fragment">The two groups are independent.</li>
  <li class="fragment">Each sample is random, or the data come from a randomized design.</li>
  <li class="fragment">If sampling without replacement, each sample should be less than 10% of its population.</li>
</ul>
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Large-count condition</span>

<p class="fragment">For each group, check successes and failures:</p>

::: {.assumption-formula .fragment}
$$
x_i \ge 10
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
n_i - x_i \ge 10.
$$
:::
:::
::::

---

## 5.4.3 Ratio of Variances

::: {.defbox .fragment}
For two normal populations, a confidence interval for $\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2$ can be written as:

$$
\left(
\frac{s_1^2/s_2^2}{F_{\alpha/2,n_1-1,n_2-1}},
\frac{s_1^2/s_2^2}{F_{1-\alpha/2,n_1-1,n_2-1}}
\right)
$$
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
This method is sensitive to non-normality. Always check whether normality is a reasonable assumption before trusting an $F$ interval for variances.
:::

---

## Example: Ratio of Variances - Machines {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
Machine 1: $n_1=16$, $s_1=12$. Machine 2: $n_2=14$, $s_2=8$.

Assuming normal populations, construct a 95% CI for $\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2$.
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

n1 <- 16; n2 <- 14
s12 <- 12^2; s22 <- 8^2
alpha <- 0.05
ratio <- s12 / s22
lower <- ratio / qf(1 - alpha/2, n1 - 1, n2 - 1)
upper <- ratio / qf(alpha/2, n1 - 1, n2 - 1)
c(lower, upper)
```

::: {.examplebox}
The 95% CI is approximately $(0.74,6.58)$. Since 1 is inside, equal variances are plausible.
:::

---

## Example: Ratio of Variances - Labs {.scrollable}

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.taskbox}
Lab 1: $n_1=21$, $s_1=5.5$. Lab 2: $n_2=19$, $s_2=3.8$.

Construct a 90% CI for $\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2$.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

n1 <- 21; n2 <- 19
s12 <- 5.5^2; s22 <- 3.8^2
alpha <- 0.10
ratio <- s12 / s22
c(
  ratio / qf(1 - alpha/2, n1 - 1, n2 - 1),
  ratio / qf(alpha/2, n1 - 1, n2 - 1)
)
```
:::
::::

::: {.examplebox}
The 90% CI is approximately $(0.96,4.51)$. Since 1 is inside, the evidence for different variances is not decisive.
:::

---

## 5.4.3.1 Ratio of Variances: Assumptions

:::: {.assumption-stack}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Required structure</span>

<ul class="assumption-list">
  <li class="fragment">The two samples are independent.</li>
  <li class="fragment">Each sample comes from a random process or randomized design.</li>
</ul>
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Normality matters here</span>

<ul class="assumption-list">
  <li class="fragment">The $F$ interval for a variance ratio is sensitive to non-normality.</li>
  <li class="fragment">This condition is more important here than it is for many mean-based intervals.</li>
</ul>
:::
::::

---

## 5.5 Paired Data

::: {.defbox .fragment}
For paired observations, reduce each pair to one difference:

$$d_i=M_{2i}-M_{1i}$$

Then construct a one-sample $t$ interval for the mean difference:

$$
\bar d \pm t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\frac{s_d}{\sqrt n}.
$$
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Use paired data when</span>
The two measurements come from the same unit, matched units, or before-after observations.
:::
::: {.warnbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Do not split the pair</span>
The pairing is information. Analyze the differences, not the two columns as independent samples.
:::
::::

---

## Example: Paired Data - Tutoring Scores {.scrollable}

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.taskbox}
Ten students take a quiz before and after tutoring. Differences are after minus before:

$$5,2,5,2,4,4,4,4,3,5$$

Construct a 95% CI for the mean improvement.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

d <- c(5,2,5,2,4,4,4,4,3,5)
mean(d)
sd(d)
t.test(d, conf.level = 0.95)
```
:::
::::

::: {.examplebox}
The 95% CI is approximately $(2.99,4.61)$ points. We are 95% confident that the mean improvement is positive.
:::

---

## Example: Paired Data - Blood Pressure {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
Twelve patients have blood pressure measured before and after treatment. Let $d=$ before minus after:

$$6,8,3,10,7,5,9,4,6,8,7,5$$

Construct a 90% CI for the mean reduction.
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

d <- c(6,8,3,10,7,5,9,4,6,8,7,5)
t.test(d, conf.level = 0.90)
```

::: {.examplebox}
The 90% CI is approximately $(5.43,7.57)$. Positive values mean the treatment lowers blood pressure on average.
:::

---

## 5.5.1 Assumptions for Paired Data

:::: {.assumption-stack}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Paired structure</span>

<ul class="assumption-list">
  <li class="fragment">Each pair comes from the same unit, matched units, or a before-after measurement.</li>
  <li class="fragment">The pairs themselves are independent of one another.</li>
</ul>
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Model condition</span>

<ul class="assumption-list">
  <li class="fragment">Analyze the differences $d_i$, not the two original columns separately.</li>
  <li class="fragment">For small samples, the distribution of the differences should be approximately normal.</li>
</ul>
:::
::::

---

## 5.6.1 Sample Size for a Mean

::: {.defbox .fragment}
If $\sigma$ is known and desired margin of error is $E$:

$$
E=z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
n=\left(\frac{z_{\alpha/2}\sigma}{E}\right)^2.
$$

Always round up.
:::

---

## Example: Sample Size for a Mean {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
A lab measurement has known $\sigma=0.0068$ grams per liter. Management wants results accurate within $E=0.005$ with 95% confidence.

How many repeated measurements are needed?
:::

$$
n=\left(\frac{1.96(0.0068)}{0.005}\right)^2=7.10
$$

::: {.examplebox}
Round up: the lab needs $n=8$ measurements.
:::

---

## Example: Sample Size for a Mean {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
A planning value is $\sigma=22.50$ and the desired margin is $E=2$.

Find the sample size for 90%, 95%, and 99% confidence.
:::

| Level | Critical value | Calculation | Required $n$ |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| 90% | 1.645 | $(1.645(22.5)/2)^2=342.41$ | 343 |
| 95% | 1.960 | $(1.960(22.5)/2)^2=486.20$ | 487 |
| 99% | 2.576 | $(2.576(22.5)/2)^2=839.45$ | 840 |

::: {.thinkbox}
Higher confidence requires a larger sample size when the desired margin of error stays fixed.
:::

---

## 5.6.1 Sample Size for a Mean: Sigma Unknown

::: {.defbox .fragment}
When $\sigma$ is unknown, use a planning estimate $s$ from a pilot study or previous data.

The practical target is:

$$
n=\left(\frac{t_{\alpha/2,n-1}s}{E}\right)^2.
$$
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Why this is iterative</span>
The $t$ critical value depends on $df=n-1$, but $n$ is what we are trying to find. A common approach is:

1. Start with the $z$ approximation.
2. Use that $n$ to find a $t$ critical value.
3. Recalculate $n$.
4. Repeat until $n$ stops changing.
:::

---

## Example: Sample Size, Sigma Unknown {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
A pilot study estimates the standard deviation of response time as $s=12$ seconds. A researcher wants a 95% CI with margin of error at most $E=5$ seconds.

Find the required sample size using the iterative $t$ approach.
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

s <- 12
E <- 5
conf <- 0.95
alpha <- 1 - conf

# Step 1: start with the z approximation
n_current <- ceiling((qnorm(1 - alpha/2) * s / E)^2)

history <- data.frame(
  step = 0,
  critical_value = qnorm(1 - alpha/2),
  n = n_current
)

for (i in 1:10) {
  tstar <- qt(1 - alpha/2, df = n_current - 1)
  n_next <- ceiling((tstar * s / E)^2)

  history <- rbind(
    history,
    data.frame(step = i, critical_value = tstar, n = n_next)
  )

  if (n_next == n_current) break
  n_current <- n_next
}

history
```

::: {.examplebox}
The sample size stabilizes at $n=25$, so the researcher needs at least 25 observations.
:::

---

## Example: Sample Size, Sigma Unknown {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
A pilot study estimates the standard deviation of monthly textbook spending as $s=18$. A 90% CI is desired with margin of error at most $E=4$.

Find the required sample size using the iterative $t$ approach.
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

s <- 18
E <- 4
conf <- 0.90
alpha <- 1 - conf

n_current <- ceiling((qnorm(1 - alpha/2) * s / E)^2)

history <- data.frame(
  step = 0,
  critical_value = qnorm(1 - alpha/2),
  n = n_current
)

for (i in 1:10) {
  tstar <- qt(1 - alpha/2, df = n_current - 1)
  n_next <- ceiling((tstar * s / E)^2)

  history <- rbind(
    history,
    data.frame(step = i, critical_value = tstar, n = n_next)
  )

  if (n_next == n_current) break
  n_current <- n_next
}

history
```

::: {.examplebox}
The sample size stabilizes at $n=57$.
:::

---

## 5.6.2 Sample Size for a Proportion

::: {.defbox .fragment}
For a desired margin of error $E$:

$$
n=\left(\frac{z^*}{E}\right)^2p^*(1-p^*)
$$

where $p^*$ is a planning value. If there is no prior information, use $p^*=0.5$.
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
The value $p^*=0.5$ is conservative because it maximizes $p^*(1-p^*)$.
:::

---

## Example: Sample Size for a Proportion {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
A mayoral survey needs to estimate a candidate's support with 95% confidence and margin of error no greater than 0.03. No prior estimate is available.
:::

$$
n=\left(\frac{1.96}{0.03}\right)^2(0.5)(0.5)=1067.11
$$

::: {.examplebox}
Round up: contact at least $n=1068$ voters.
:::

---

## Example: Sample Size for a Proportion {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
In 2007, 15.6% of people in the USA were not covered by health care insurance. Use $p^*=0.156$ and $E=0.03$.

Find the required sample size for 95% and 99% confidence.
:::

$$
n_{95}=\left(\frac{1.96}{0.03}\right)^2(0.156)(0.844)=562.54\Rightarrow563
$$

$$
n_{99}=\left(\frac{2.576}{0.03}\right)^2(0.156)(0.844)=970.97\Rightarrow971
$$

::: {.examplebox}
The 99% confidence level requires a larger survey because the critical value is larger.
:::

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

When calculating sample size from a margin of error, why do we round up?
::::

- Because formulas always underestimate the standard deviation
- [Because sample size must be whole, and rounding down could make the margin of error too large]{.correct data-explanation="The target is a maximum margin of error. Rounding down can fail to meet the requirement, so we always round up."}
- Because confidence intervals require even sample sizes
- Because $z^*$ is only approximate

---

## Choosing the Right CI {.compact}

| If the problem asks for... | Use... |
|---|---|
| one mean and gives $\sigma$ | one-sample $z$ interval |
| one mean and gives $s$ or raw data | one-sample $t$ interval |
| one proportion | one-proportion $z$ interval |
| one variance | chi-square interval |
| difference of means, known $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$ | two-sample $z$ interval |
| difference of means, equal variances | pooled two-sample $t$ interval |
| difference of means, unequal/unspecified variances | Welch two-sample $t$ interval |
| difference of proportions | two-proportion $z$ interval |
| ratio of variances | $F$ interval |
| before-after or matched data | paired $t$ interval on differences |

---

## Final Checklist

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Before calculating</span>
- Identify the parameter.
- Check one sample vs two sample vs paired.
- Check whether the target is a mean, proportion, or variance.
- Pick the reference distribution.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">After calculating</span>
- Include units when relevant.
- Interpret in context.
- Check whether 0 or 1 has a special meaning.
- For sample size, round up.
:::
::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**One slide takeaway.** Confidence intervals are not separate tricks. They are the same idea with different estimators, standard errors, and reference distributions.
:::
